title: two propagations in one compound expression compile and run, and the second one never runs after the first fails
notes: RETIRED REFUSAL, kept under its old filename so the COVERAGE.md rows that cite it keep resolving. specification/failures.mdx §Refusal Conditions withdrew the five-condition placement walk; see DECISIONS.md §Typed failures. WHY IT NOW PASSES, and it is the clearest demonstration in the corpus of what the withdrawn rule was actually protecting: `scoreOf("ada")! + scoreOf("bob")!` has TWO propagations, and BOTH hoist, in authored order. The emitted statement calls `scoreOf("ada")`, checks it, calls `scoreOf("bob")`, checks it, and only then adds — which is exactly the authored order, so nothing was reordered by admitting it. The stdout is the proof rather than a formality: `bob` is missing, and the program prints that failure, which can only happen if the second guard ran after the second call and not before the first. Contrast `precededByUnhoistedEffect` in poc/src/language/semantic.ts, which still refuses `g() + r!`: there the left operand leaves an effect the lowering does NOT hoist, so the guard would jump in front of it. Two operands, one operator, opposite verdicts — and the difference is what is to the left, not where the `!` sits. MARKER RETIRED 2026-08-30, and the fork's half of the withdrawal is what retired it. `safeUnwrapPlacement` and `isInRepeatedLoopHeader` are deleted from `compiler/forkbridge/lowering.go.txt` and replaced by the SAME three predicates the reference applies — `conditionallyEvaluatedPosition`, `repeatedlyEvaluatedPosition` and `precededByUnhoistedEffect` — so both backends now accept this program for the same stated reason. Re-derived by RUNNING both backends over this case, not by reading either one's source: the fork's predicates were written against measured behaviour and checked against the reference on the three programs that keep the residue alive (`while (next()!) {}`, `maybe ?? r!`, `g() + r!`), each of which both backends still refuse with the same code at the same position. This case is the one where the fork had the most to prove, because it holds TWO propagation points in one statement: the guard for `scoreOf("bob")` is hoisted behind the guard for `scoreOf("ada")`, in authored order, which is exactly what `precededByUnhoistedEffect` permits by treating a nested propagation as free. `compiler/fork_internal_lowering_test.go` pins the emitted order on the fork side.
